plan: [ This is strategically equivalent to a second‑price auction: the highest sealed bid wins and pays the second-highest bid. In such auctions, bidding one’s true value is a dominant strategy—it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ strategies. Overbidding risks winning at a price above value; underbidding risks losing when winning would have yielded positive surplus. There is only 1 round and no history to learn from, so no adjustments are needed. Therefore, bid exactly my private value to ensure I win whenever price is below or equal to my value and avoid negative surplus. ]

[ This mechanism is strategically equivalent to a sealed-bid second-price auction: the winner pays the second-highest sealed bid. In such auctions, bidding your true private value is a (weakly) dominant strategy. Underbidding risks losing when the second-highest bid is below my value, reducing expected profit; overbidding risks paying above my value if I win. There is no prior history to exploit and only 1 round, with values i.i.d. uniform. To maximize expected long-run profit (here, this round), bid my value: 17. ]

[ This is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction: the winner pays the second-highest bid. The weakly dominant strategy is to bid my true value. Overbidding risks negative profit if I win above value; underbidding risks losing when I would have profited. Ties are random but do not change optimality. With values i.i.d. each round and only one round, there’s no gain from strategic shading or signaling. Therefore, I will set my sealed bid equal to my value to maximize expected profit. ]
